source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's Durham campus publishes 40 MW of IT capacity across 420,000 square feet, making it the anchor of North Carolina's published data center capacity.

The two numbers together describe a conventional hall, not an extreme one. Forty megawatts spread over 420,000 square feet of technical space is about 95 watts per square foot. That density suits standard enterprise and cloud deployment. Whether the halls are built for the higher rack densities that current AI accelerators require is not published, and the operator lists no rack count, no accelerator count, and no power usage effectiveness.

The state context is what makes the campus notable. It ranks first among the five North Carolina facilities that publish a megawatt figure, and those five together publish 50.266 MW, so this one campus accounts for roughly 80 percent of the state's published capacity. North Carolina has 19 mapped facilities, and most publish no figure at all, so the published total is a floor rather than a census. Under either a 40 kW or a 100 kW per-rack assumption, this is the only facility in the state whose published number is large enough to host a meaningful training cluster.

What the data does not cover matters as much as what it does. The spec page carries no address, no postal code, and no certifications, so nothing here establishes which compliance regimes the campus qualifies for, who its tenants are, or what power it draws beyond the IT figure. The rack counts above are assumptions about density, not claims by CyrusOne. A single facility's published capacity also says nothing about the grid that feeds it, the generation behind that grid, or how long an interconnection would take, which are the constraints that decide whether 40 MW can actually be delivered to accelerators.
